content: The decision-making procedures were established at the beginning of the meetings, including a minimal set of rules for agreement and voting. At least two-thirds of the guideline development group needed to be present for the initial discussion of evidence and proposed recommendations. The group voted in secret on the direction and strength of the recommendations using a specially designed form. This form also included sections for documenting their views on the intervention's desirable and undesirable effects, the quality of available evidence, values and preferences in different settings, and the cost of options available to healthcare workers. Each member had one vote unless otherwise advised, and abstentions were not allowed. Any potential conflicts of interest were managed beforehand. The WHO Secretariat collected the voting forms and disclosed a summary of the results to the group. If unanimous consensus was not reached, additional time was allocated for deliberations, and a second round of voting could occur. If full agreement was still not achieved, a two-thirds majority vote was required for approval. Divergent opinions, if any, were recorded in the guideline. Voting forms were retained by WHO for 10 years. Consensus was ultimately reached for all recommendations. WHO staff and external technical experts involved in evidence collection and grading were not allowed to vote. There were no strong disagreements among the group members. A draft of the revised principles and recommendations was disseminated for external peer review in February 2012. Reviewers were asked to examine the principles and recommendations to ensure no important omissions, contradictions, or inconsistencies with scientific evidence or programmatic feasibility. They were also asked to clarify the language, particularly regarding implementation and how policymakers and program staff might interpret the recommendations. Reviewers were informed that no additional recommendations could be considered and that they were participating in their personal capacity, not as representatives of any agency or institution. External reviewers provided comments to make the recommendations clearer, and there was no major disagreement. The draft principles and recommendations were circulated to all involved WHO technical staff, regional TB advisers, selected national TB programs, technical agencies working on TB control, and a network of external experts in TB and nutrition. All interested stakeholders became members of the external experts’ and stakeholders’ panel but were only allowed to comment on the draft guideline after submitting a signed declaration of interests form. Feedback was received from these stakeholders, and WHO staff addressed each comment before finalizing the guideline and submitting it for clearance prior to publication. According to WHO rules, all experts participating in meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before their participation. Conflict of interest statements for all guideline group members were reviewed by the responsible technical officer and relevant departments before finalizing the group composition and inviting members to attend meetings. All participants submitted a declaration of interests form and their curriculum vitae before each meeting. They also verbally declared any interests at the beginning of each meeting and agreed to the publication of their declarations if relevant. The procedures for managing conflicts of interest strictly followed WHO guidelines. Upon reviewing the responses, none of the declared interests were deemed likely to influence the discussions, and no special provisions were considered necessary. External experts representing partner organizations, representatives from the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development, the Global TB Programme, and selected national TB programs participated in the meetings and review processes. All external experts were required to submit a curriculum vitae and complete a declaration of interest form. Systematic reviews were conducted to address specific questions, such as the optimal diet composition for patients receiving treatment for active TB, the role of macronutrient and micronutrient supplementation in improving TB treatment outcomes, and the potential for population-level nutritional interventions to reduce the progression from latent to active TB. The findings on diet composition were integrated into the guideline's background section, focusing on energy requirements. However, evidence on energy requirements in TB patients was limited, with only two observational studies involving 40 TB patients. These studies suggested a 14% higher basal metabolic rate in TB patients compared to controls, but the evidence quality was very low. Regarding macronutrient supplementation, five trials assessed the provision of free food or high-energy supplements, but none demonstrated a total daily caloric intake above the recommended levels for non-infected populations. The trials were too small to reliably determine clinical benefits on mortality, TB cure, or treatment completion. One small trial in India showed a statistically significant benefit in treatment completion and bacterial clearance, but these findings were not confirmed in larger trials. Moderate-quality evidence suggested that free food or high-energy nutritional products might modestly increase weight gain during treatment. Two small studies on TB-HIV co-infected individuals indicated potential improvements in physical function and quality of life, but the evidence was of low quality. For micronutrient supplementation, five trials assessed multi-micronutrient supplementation at doses up to 10 times the dietary reference intake, and 12 trials assessed single or dual micronutrient supplementation. There was insufficient evidence to determine whether multi-micronutrients had a beneficial effect on mortality in HIV-negative TB patients, but moderate-quality evidence suggested little or no effect on mortality in HIV-positive TB patients. No studies assessed the effects of multi-micronutrients on TB cure or treatment completion. Multi-micronutrient supplements likely had little or no effect on the proportion of TB patients remaining sputum-positive during the first eight weeks or on weight gain during treatment. Plasma levels of certain vitamins and minerals, such as zinc, vitamin D, vitamin E, and selenium, may improve with supplementation during early TB treatment, but consistent beneficial effects on TB treatment outcomes or nutritional recovery were not demonstrated. A literature review investigated whether poor nutritional status in household contacts increased the risk of developing active TB. Six studies were identified, with two suggesting that malnutrition and younger age increased the risk of active TB in household contacts. However, the evidence was limited, and no intervention studies were included. It remains unclear whether nutritional supplementation reduces the risk of progression from latent to active TB or improves health outcomes in TB patients. The overall evidence base on nutritional supplements for TB prevention and care is weak. The recommendations in this guideline align with WHO's general recommendations on nutritional care and support, as there is no strong evidence to suggest that TB patients require different nutritional care than others. Future research should focus on nutrient requirements, supplementation effects, and the impact of implementing WHO's nutrition and TB recommendations.
